blocks.text: The marked structure in the image is the Yolk sac. The Midgut of the embryo communicates with the yolk sac via a stalk called the Vitelline duct. Yolk sac: Description A small membranous structure outside the embryo. The yolk sac connects to the developing embryo at midgut via the vitelline duct. (Option B) The primitive yolk sac is lined by Hypoblast cells, which is derived from Endoderm (forms the first lining).
Functions
Primitive hematopoiesis Germ cell production. Nutritive role (before blood vessels form)
Development

The primary yolk sac forms from proliferating hypoblast cells after implantation, while the epiblast forms the amnion. Both structures develop between days 8-14 of embryogenesis. Hypoblast cells are continuous with the exocoelomic membrane.

By the end of the second week, extraembryonic mesoderm fills the space between the trophoblast, amnion, and exocoelomic membrane. As vacuoles form within this tissue, the extraembryonic coelom or chorionic cavity develops. The extraembryonic mesoderm lining the cytotrophoblast and amnion is called extraembryonic somatic mesoderm, while the lining around the yolk sac is the extraembryonic splanchnic mesoderm.

The primary yolk sac enlarges, part of it regresses, and the remaining portion forms the secondary yolk sac. Portions of the secondary yolk sac not taken up inside the embryo forms the tertiary yolk sac.
Visualization Timeline
Although the yolk sac forms in the second week, it is visible on ultrasound by 5 weeks post-fertilization (or 7 gestational weeks). Growth is linear between 5-10 weeks post-fertilization.
Not visible after the first trimester.

**Foregut (Option A):** The foregut is initially bounded by the oropharyngeal membrane, which separates the stomodeum (primitive oral cavity) from the pharynx. The membrane ruptures in the 4th week, establishing an open connection between the oral cavity and primitive gut.

**Hindgut (Option C):** and Cloacal membrane (Option D): The hindgut terminates at the cloacal membrane, which separates the upper anal canal (endodermal) from the lower proctodeum (ectodermal). The membrane breaks down in the 7th week to create the anal opening. Cephalocaudal growth and lateral folding incorporate part of the allantois into the embryo, forming the cloaca.

Occipital somites contribute to the formation of the muscles of the tongue. Paraxial Mesoderm: Extends as a longitudinal column on either side of the notochord and the developing neural tube. Developing otic capsules (neuroectodermal thickenings that form the membranous labyrinth of the internal ear) divide the paraxial mesoderm into preotic and postotic parts. Preotic Paraxial Mesoderm: Comprises unsegmented head mesoderm, known as somitomeres.

Postotic Paraxial Mesoderm: Forms somites Somites: Paraxial mesoderm becomes segmented to form 42-44 pairs of somites develop on either side of the neural tube and notochord. Appear between the 20th and 30th day, marking the 4th week as the somite period. Somite Structure: Sclerotome: Ventromedial part; forms vertebral column and ribs. Dermatome: Lateral part; forms dermis of skin and subcutaneous tissue.

Myotome: Intermediate part; forms striated muscle. Innervation: Cervical, thoracic, lumbar, and sacral regions: One spinal nerve innervates each myotome (no. of somites = no. of spinal nerves). Coccygeal region: Somites
exceed spinal nerves and many degenerate.

rows: Striated muscles of trunk, diaphragm, limbs

items.text: The lamina terminalis is the part of the neural tube wall that closes the cranial end of the prosencephalon. (Option C)
It lies in the anterior wall of the third ventricle after the appearance of the telencephalic vesicles. (Option A)

blocks.text: The lamina terminalis forms the commissural plate, which allows neural fibers to pass between hemispheres.
Commissural fibers:

items.text: Hippocampal commissure/fornix (second). Corpus callosum (largest, forms later and extends backward, roofing over the diencephalon). The septum pellucidum persists from the portion of the lamina terminalis between the corpus callosum and fornix. (Option B)

blocks.text: Other commissures include the optic chiasma, habenular commissure, and posterior commissure.

The stomatodeum (future mouth) is a depression bounded cranially by a bulging produced by the brain, and caudally by a bulging produced by the pericardial cavity. It is derived from the ectoderm. It forms the oral epithelium, including the lips, teeth, and part of the palate.
**Endoderm (Option B):** contributes to the internal lining of the gastrointestinal tract but is not responsible for the stomatodeum.
**Mesoderm (Option C):** contributes to structures such as muscles and connective tissues but not to the stomatodeum directly.
**Neural Crest Cells (Option D):** contribute to structures like the face and skull but do not form the stomatodeum.
The development of the lungs follows a well-defined sequence:

items.text: Pseudoglandular phase (5–16 weeks): Formation of terminal bronchioles.
Canalicular phase (16–26 weeks): Formation of respiratory bronchioles and capillary networks.
Saccular phase (26–36 weeks): Formation of primitive alveoli and and capillaries establish close contact.
Alveolar phase (36 weeks–postnatal): Formation of mature alveoli and blood-air barrier.

blocks.text: Premature Birth and RDS: The onset of surfactant production in the canalicular phase and its increase during the saccular phase is essential for preventing alveolar collapse. Premature infants born before 34 weeks are at significant risk for Respiratory Distress Syndrome (RDS) due to insufficient surfactant production and immature alveolar development. Treatment includes surfactant replacement therapy and supportive ventilation.
The alveolar epithelial cells (Type I and Type II) are derived from the endoderm of the laryngotracheal tube.
Derivatives of the Laryngotracheal Tube:
The laryngotracheal tube develops from the foregut and gives rise to critical structures in the respiratory system.
Endodermal Derivatives:
Endoderm: Forms the lining of the larynx, trachea, bronchi, and alveoli, including the Type I and Type II alveolar cells.
Mesodermal Derivatives:
Splanchnic Mesoderm: Forms the cartilage, smooth muscle, and visceral pleura of the respiratory tract. Somatic Mesoderm: Forms the parietal pleura lining the thoracic cavity.
Developmental Stages:
4th week: The lung bud appears as an outgrowth from the foregut. 4-5th weeks: The tracheoesophageal septum forms, separating the foregut into the trachea and esophagus.
Subsequent weeks: Primary, secondary, and tertiary bronchi form, leading to the adult bronchopulmonary segments.

The Post-renal (Infra-renal) segment of the Inferior vena cava (IVC) develops primarily from the right supracardinal vein. Formation of IVC: The beginning of the IVC is called the Posterior cardinal vein. Posterior cardinal vein contributes to Sacro cardinal vein. Kidneys drain into the inferior vena cava with the help of renal veins.

Right supracardinal vein contributes the Post-renal (infra-renal) segment of the IVC. Right subcardinal vein contributes the Renal and Pre-renal (suprarenal) segment of IVC. Terminal portion of the IVC is contributed by the right sided vitelline veins. The right sided vitelline veins will contribute to the right Hepatiocardiac channel. All this happen in the right side whereas Left sided veins will disappear.
There is Anastomosis between:
A persistent left-sided SVC arises from the left anterior cardinal vein, which typically regresses during fetal development.
Normal Development:

The right anterior cardinal vein forms the right SVC. The left anterior cardinal vein regresses, with its remnant forming the left brachiocephalic vein, which connects the left and right venous systems.
Persistent Left-Sided SVC:
Occurs due to the failure of the left anterior cardinal vein to regress.
This results in the formation of a left-sided SVC, which drains into the right atrium through the coronary sinus. The right SVC typically develops normally.
Double SVC:
If the left brachiocephalic vein fails to form, the left anterior cardinal vein persists as a separate venous channel.

In this condition: The right anterior cardinal vein forms the right SVC. The left anterior cardinal vein persists as the left SVC. A. Left superior vena cava draining into the right atrium by way of the coronary sinus B. Double superior vena cava. The communicating [brachiocephalic] vein between the two anterior cardinals has failed to develop
The structure “c” is decidua parietalis that fuses with the growing decidua capsularis around the embryo.
Three types of decidua:

This forms the maternal component of the placenta The maternal spiral arteries grow and dilate to form sinusoids with blood Contains large decidual cells rich in lipids and glycogen (may be a source of nutrition for the embryo) Firmly attached to the chorion Separates the embryo from the uterine cavity Covers the embryo like a capsule Lines the rest of the uterine cavity With the progression of the pregnancy, the decidua capsularis grows with the fetus and finally fuses with the parietalis during the 3rd month and obliterates the uterine cavity.
The decidua is eventually shed off with the placenta and membranes after delivery.
**Myometrium (Option C):** is labelled as structure "d" in the image

The tertiary villi are formed with the extraembryonic mesoderm core filled with fetal blood, which establishes the fetoplacental circulation. The chorion is formed by the extraembryonic somatic mesoderm, cytotrophoblast, and syncytiotrophoblast. The chorionic villi formed from the chorion cover the chorionic sac (extraembryonic coelom) until the beginning of the 8th week.
According to the structure of the chorionic villi at different periods of embryonic development they are divided into:
A central core of cytotrophoblast (Option D) covered by a layer of syncytiotrophoblast. Intervillous space separates the villus from each other.
Has 3 layers:
Similar to secondary villi but have fetal blood capillaries in the mesoderm
Formation of the villi:
Appearance of lacunae and trabeculae (around the 12th day of gestation): Small cavities appear in the rapidly growing and thick syncytiotrophoblast.

These cavities are called lacunae and they increase in size and arrange themselves from irregular to a radial design around the blastocyst. The syncytium separates them from one another, forming partitions called trabeculae, which in time get surrounded by lacunae as they communicate with each other and one large space is formed.
Erosion of maternal endometrium:

The endometrium of the maternal uterus is eroded by the growing syncytiotrophoblasts, which leads to the opening of some blood vessels and the leaking of blood into the lacunar space (uteroplacental circulation). (Option B)
Formation of chorionic villi:

Once the cytotrophoblast grows into the trabeculae, it becomes a two-layered structure with a core of cytotrophoblast covered by a layer of syncytiotrophoblast and surrounded by maternal blood in the lacunar space.

The trabeculae have now become the primary villi and the lacunar space, the intervillous space. When the extraembryonic mesoderm invades this primary villus and forms the core, this structure becomes the secondary villi, with the mesoderm core covered by cytotrophoblast and then the syncytiotrophoblast. Once the blood vessels fill the mesoderm, the tertiary villi are formed.
The maternal blood runs in the intervillous space, and the fetal blood in the villi.

The placental membrane or barrier separates the maternal and fetal blood in the intrauterine period but thins out towards the end of pregnancy for many reasons, one of which is the disappearance of the cytotrophoblast. Placenta has 2 parts (maternal and fetal), 2 surfaces (maternal and fetal), 2 types of cotyledons, and a peripheral margin. Maternal part is formed by the decidua basalis or decidual plate of the endometrium.

Fetal part is from the chorion frondosum or chorionic plate. Maternal surface is rough and irregular having maternal cotyledons. Fetal surface is smooth and covered by amnion. Peripheral margin of the placenta presents the fetal membrane formed from decidua capsularis and pareitalis, chorion laeve and amnion.

Placental Membrane: This separates the fetal blood in the villi from the maternal blood in the intervillous space running side by side but opposite in direction. The exchange of oxygen, nutrition, and waste products occurs through this membrane.
The following are the structures that form the placental membrane early in pregnancy:

items.text: Endothelium of maternal blood vessels and its basement membrane
Endothelium of fetal blood vessels and its basement membrane

blocks.text: Structures that form the placental membrane Later in pregnancy:

items.text: Endothelium of fetal capillaries and their basement membrane (Option B & C)

blocks.text: The placental membrane thins later in pregnancy due to:

items.text: Peripheral migration of fetal blood vessels

blocks.text: The total area of this membrane varies from 4 meter-squared to 14 meter-squared and is 0.025mm thick at first and later 0.002mm.
The structure marked “C” is Chorion, which is formed by the parietal (or somatopleuric) extraembryonic mesoderm and the trophoblast.
Formation of extraembryonic mesoderm:
Extra embryonic mesoderm, also called the primary mesoderm, is a mass of cells formed from the cells of the yolk sac cells (Hueser’s membrane) and lies outside the embryonic disc.
This separates the endodermal layer covering the yolk sac and the trophoblast, as well as the wall of the amniotic cavity from the trophoblast. It does not form any tissues of the embryo.
Formation of extraembryonic coelom:

The extraembryonic mesoderm develops small cavities that later coalesce into one large cavity called the extraembryonic coelom (chorionic cavity), which divides the extraembryonic mesoderm into two layers.

The layer between the amniotic cavity and the inside of the trophoblast is the parietal or somatopleuric extraembryonic mesoderm, and the layer outside the yolk sac is called the visceral or splanchnopleuric extraembryonic mesoderm.
Formation of connecting stalk:
The part of the extraembryonic mesoderm that keeps the amniotic sac, embryo, and yolk sac attached to the trophoblast, develops a structure called the connecting stalk.
Formation of chorion and amnion:

The parietal (or somatopleuric) extraembryonic mesoderm, cytotrophoblast and syncytiotrophoblast form a membrane called the chorion. The amniogenic cells of the walls of the amniotic cavity and the parietal extraembryonic mesoderm form the amnion. The amnion and chorion play a major role in childbirth.
